title: Benchmarking your code
text:
A benchmark is a small, controlled test of your code that you can use to predict what the full project will need. The goal is not to run everything, but to run just enough to learn how time and memory change as the problem grows.

The benchmarking workflow

Create representative test cases: smaller versions of your real problem, using the same type of data and the same code path
Test the scaling: run with several sizes (e.g. 2%, 4% and 8% of the data) and see how the time grows
Extrapolate carefully: use the scaling you observed to predict the full problem, and add safety factors







Good habits




Document your environment: software versions, loaded modules, and the machine you used
Run end-to-end tests, including every step (reading the data, computing, writing results), because I/O can be a significant cost
Benchmark on the same type of hardware you will use for the real runs





Essential measurement tools

GNU time
The GNU time command runs your program and reports the resources it used. Note that you need to call it by its full path, /usr/bin/time, because most shells have a simpler built-in command with the same name.
# Basic timing with detailed output
/usr/bin/time -v my_program input.dat

# Custom format for logging
/usr/bin/time -f 'wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS=%M' my_program input.dat








Output
Format code
Meaning




Elapsed (wall-clock) time
%e (seconds) or %E (h:mm:ss)
What a stopwatch would measure


User time
%U
CPU time spent in your code


System time
%S
CPU time spent in the operating system on your behalf (e.g. reading files)


Maximum resident set size
%M
Peak memory used, in kilobytes









Note



If /usr/bin/time is not available (for example on macOS), the shell built-in time my_program still gives you the elapsed, user and system times, but not the memory. In Python you can read the peak memory of a process with the standard resource module, as the exercise script of this course does.





Example: benchmark script
The script below runs a program with three different data sizes and saves the measurements to a log file, so they can be analysed later:
#!/bin/bash

for size in 2 4 8; do
    echo "Testing ${size}% data size..."
    /usr/bin/time -o benchmark_results.log -a \
        -f "size=${size}pct wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS_KB=%M" \
        my_simulation --input data_${size}pct.csv \
                      --output results_${size}pct.dat
done
The options -o benchmark_results.log -a tell time to append its report to the log file, which keeps the measurements separate from anything your program prints.

Allowing for sources of variability
Run times are never exactly the same twice: other users share the node or the file system, and your own code may use random numbers. Particularly when your tests are short, you should repeat each measurement a few times, for example by adding an extra nested loop:
for size in 2 4 8; do
    for run in 1 2 3; do
        /usr/bin/time -o benchmark_results.log -a \
            -f "size=${size}pct run=${run} wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS_KB=%M" \
            my_simulation --input data_${size}pct.csv \
                          --output results_${size}pct_run${run}.dat
    done
done



Worked example: image processing






Scenario



An image processing pipeline that

loads images from disk,
runs an object detection model, and
saves the results.

Goal: process 10,000 images and estimate the resources needed.



Step 1: create test datasets
Make smaller subsets of the full dataset by random sampling, so that they are representative of the whole:
# Create subsets of your full dataset
mkdir test_data_5pct test_data_10pct test_data_15pct

# Randomly sample (adjust the numbers for your case)
shuf -n 500  full_image_list.txt > test_data_5pct/image_list.txt
shuf -n 1000 full_image_list.txt > test_data_10pct/image_list.txt
shuf -n 1500 full_image_list.txt > test_data_15pct/image_list.txt


Step 2: run the benchmarks
#!/bin/bash
module load languages/python/3.7.12

for size in 5 10 15; do
    echo "=== Testing ${size}% dataset ==="
    for run in 1 2 3; do
        echo "Run $run..."
        /usr/bin/time -o timing_results.log -a \
            -f "${size}pct run${run}: wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS_KB=%M" \
            python image_pipeline.py \
                --input test_data_${size}pct/ \
                --output results_${size}pct_run${run}/
    done
done


Step 3: analyse the results
# Extract the timing data
grep "wall=" timing_results.log
5pct run1:  wall=135.21 user=121.45 sys=12.33 maxRSS_KB=2048000
5pct run2:  wall=138.04 user=123.12 sys=13.01 maxRSS_KB=2051000
5pct run3:  wall=134.77 user=120.88 sys=12.40 maxRSS_KB=2049000
10pct run1: wall=270.55 user=243.90 sys=24.78 maxRSS_KB=2052000
...
15pct run1: wall=405.38 user=366.22 sys=36.51 maxRSS_KB=2055000
...
Averaging the three runs of each size gives



Data used
Wall time
Compared with 5%




5%
~135 s
1×


10%
~270 s
2×


15%
~405 s
3×



Doubling and tripling the data doubled and tripled the time, so the scaling is linear. The memory barely changes (about 2 GB in every case), so it does not depend on how many images we process. Extrapolating to the whole dataset (100%, i.e. 20 times the 5% test):
\[
135 \text{ s} \times 20 = 2700 \text{ s} = 45 \text{ minutes}
\]
and we should ask for about 2 GB of memory (plus a safety margin) for the job.



If it is not linear
If the times do not grow in proportion to the data size, you can fit a curve through your measurements and use it to predict the full-size runtime. A polynomial of order 2 or 3 is generally a good option for capturing non-linear trends. You can do this in a spreadsheet (add a trendline to the chart and choose to display the equation) or in a few lines of Python:
import numpy as np

percent = np.array([5, 10, 15, 20])
wall = np.array([40.0, 95.0, 170.0, 265.0])   # seconds

coeffs = np.polyfit(percent, wall, deg=2)     # quadratic trend
prediction = np.polyval(coeffs, 100)          # forecast for 100% of the data
print(f"Predicted wall time with all the data: {prediction / 60:.0f} minutes")



Benchmark times with a quadratic trendline extrapolated to the full dataset








Warning



Extrapolating far beyond the range you measured is risky: here we predict at 100% from tests that stop at 20%, and small differences in the fit become large differences in the forecast. Use more test sizes (or larger ones) when your tests are a small fraction of the full problem, and always add a safety factor when converting the prediction to a resource request.


Benchmarking on HPC systems

title: Remote working
text:
The original super-power of the command line is that it allows us to connect to other machines. While today we have remote-desktops and screen-shares to see and work with other computer’s GUIs, the command line has been doing this since the 1960s!
In research, we often work on remote machines (“computing clusters”, “HPC”, “supercomputers”, or even just “servers”), which we need to log in to. Once we are logged in, the terminal will behave as if we are sitting at that machine, which might be on the other side of the world.

Using ssh
SSH is the primary method for connecting to HPC systems. ssh command opens a command line session on a remote computer. The name is short for “secure shell”, because it opens a shell to communicate with a remote machine on the same network, using an encrypted, secure connection.
ssh us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk
After executing something like the above command, you will then be asked to enter your password - it will not display anything or display stars (*) as you type. If the password is correct, you will then see a new prompt, including the name of the machine you are now logged in to, for example:
[us01234@hpc-server ~]$
ssh can be used for more than just remote login, it can also execute commands remotely without starting an interactive session.

Using PuTTY
PuTTY is a popular, open source SSH client for Windows. It can be downloaded here.



PuTTY configuration interface.





Copying files to and from remote machines using scp
SCP uses SSH to transfer files securely between systems. scp (“secure copy”) is just like cp, except it can copy files and folders to and from another computer. scp is built on top of SSH and provides a secure way to transfer files, ensuring data confidentiality during transit.
Just like with cp, you can copy the contents of folders with the flag -r.
# Copy local file to remote host
scp local_file.txt us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk:/remote/path/

# Copy remote file to local system
scp us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk:/remote/file.txt /local/path/

# Copy entire directory recursively
scp -r /local/directory us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk:/remote/path/
If you don’t have scp in your Windows machine, you can download it from PuTTY’s website.


FileZilla for Graphical File Transfer
FileZilla provides a user-friendly graphical interface for file transfers. It is available at the Company Portal.

Setting up FileZilla Connection

Open FileZilla and go to File → Site Manager
Create New Site with these settings:

Protocol: SFTP - SSH File Transfer Protocol
Host: Your HPC system hostname, e.g. hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk
Port: 22 (or your system’s SSH port)
Logon Type:

“Normal” for password authentication
“Key file” for SSH key authentication

User: Your username, e.g. us01234





FileZilla interface.




Using FileZilla

Left panel: Your local computer files
Right panel: Remote HPC system files

Transfer files: Drag and drop between panels
Queue: Monitor transfer progress in bottom panel




FileZilla interface with a connection established.





SSH Key Authentication
Setting up SSH keys eliminates the need to type passwords repeatedly.
To generate a key you can type on your Terminal (Mac) or PowerShell (Windows):
# Generate SSH key pair on your local machine
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096
Then you need to copy the key to the server using:
# Copy public key to HPC system
ssh-copy-id us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk
Or if you don’t have ssh-copy-id in your system, you can do it manually:

Copy your key to the clipboard.


Windows (powershell)Mac & Linux


type $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_rsa.pub
``


cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub




Connect to the server

ssh us01234@hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk

On the server, run the following instructions replacing YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY with the key you have copied in your clipboard.

echo "YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY" >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
``

SSH Configuration File
Create ~/.ssh/config on your local machine to simplify connections:
# To connect simply with 'ssh hpc-server'
Host hpc-server
    HostName hpc-server.bristol.ac.uk
    User us01234
    Port 22
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa

title: Converting benchmarks to resource requests
text:
Once you have a set of benchmark measurements, the last step is to turn them into the numbers you will put in your job scripts (per-job requests) and in your project proposal or allocation request (total core-hours).

From benchmarks to core-hours

Pick a scaling model from your test results (linear, quadratic, …)
Extrapolate to the full problem size
Choose the parallel configuration with a good balance between speed and efficiency (see the parallel scaling results: more cores are not always better value)
Calculate the core-hours per run
Multiply by the number of runs (tasks, parameter sets, repetitions…)
Add safety factors



Safety factors
A benchmark is a prediction, and predictions are wrong. Typical reasons to add a margin are







Reason
Example factor




Failed or repeated jobs (crashes, jobs that run out of time, queue problems)
1.4×


Development and testing as the project evolves, extra analyses or reruns
2.0×


Errors in the scaling extrapolation
1.2×



The factors are multiplied: 1.4 × 2.0 × 1.2 = 3.36. These are just examples; use your own judgement, with larger margins when the extrapolation is longer or the code is less predictable.






Warning



Request memory and run time in your job scripts with some margin too, since a job that exceeds either limit is killed and its work is lost. But do not overdo it: a very generous time limit can make your job wait longer in the queue.




Worked example: climate study






Scenario






Program
climate_sim


Test data
20% of the full grid (1 simulated year)


Hardware
8 cores, 75% parallel efficiency


Measured time
45 minutes of wall-clock time


Scaling
Linear with the size of the grid


Parameter sets
50 different configurations






Resource calculation

Full problem: 5× larger than the test (20% → 100%)
Time per run: 45 min × 5 = 225 min = 3.75 hours
Core-hours per run: 3.75 h × 8 cores = 30 core-hours
Base cost: 30 core-hours × 50 runs = 1,500 core-hours
Safety factors: 1.4 × 2.0 × 1.2 = 3.36
Total request: 1,500 × 3.36 = 5,040 core-hours

The measured 45 minutes already includes the 75% parallel efficiency, because it was measured on 8 cores. The efficiency would only be needed if you wanted to predict the time with a different number of cores.






What goes in the job script?



For each individual run, the numbers above suggest a job with --cpus-per-task=8 and a time limit of at least 3.75 hours, so something like --time=05:00:00 leaves a reasonable margin. The 50 runs can be submitted together as an array job.


Hands-on exercise

title: Exercise: estimating resources
text:
In this exercise you will benchmark a small Python program, find out how its run time and memory use grow with the size of the data, and use your measurements to estimate the resources needed for a larger project, following the steps of the previous pages.
Time needed: about 30 minutes, most of it waiting for the benchmarks to run.

The problem
The program neighbour_counts.py reads a cloud of points in 3D space and counts, for every point, how many other points lie within a given distance of it. It is the kind of calculation you find in spatial statistics, clustering and particle simulations. It uses only the Python standard library.
The dataset, points.csv, is small: 30,000 points in a file of less than 1 MB. But the program compares every point with every other point, so the cost does not come from the size of the file. A single run on the whole dataset takes a couple of minutes.
You will need these files:

points.csv: the dataset (columns id,x,y,z)
neighbour_counts.py: the program
make_points.py: generates a dataset of any size (only needed if you want to experiment)

Download them to your working directory on the HPC system, for example with
wget https://bristol-training.github.io/intro-hpc/data/points.csv
wget https://bristol-training.github.io/intro-hpc/data/neighbour_counts.py






Important



Remember: do not run the benchmarks on the login node. Either request an interactive session on a compute node,
salloc --partition=test --nodes=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00
or submit the commands as a batch job, as shown in Task 2.




Task 1: a first measurement
Load a Python module and run the program once on the full dataset, measuring it with GNU time:
module load languages/python/3.7.12

/usr/bin/time -v python neighbour_counts.py points.csv
The program prints a short summary of the results and, at the end, its own timing report. The time -v report appears below that.
Write down, from the time -v output:



Quantity
Your value




Elapsed (wall clock) time



User time + system time (CPU time)



Maximum resident set size (peak memory)










Questions




Is the program using more than one core? (Compare the CPU time with the wall-clock time.)
How many core-hours did this run use?
If you wanted to run it as a job, how much memory would you ask for?









Solution





The numbers depend on the processor of the node, but you should see something like this:

Wall-clock time of about 2 minutes (136 s in our test), and user time almost identical to it: the CPU time is about the same as the wall time, so the program is using one core
Core-hours: 136 s × 1 core ÷ 3600 = about 0.04 core-hours
Peak memory of less than 20 MB (Maximum resident set size is reported in kilobytes). This is mostly Python itself and the list of points; the program needs very little memory, so a request of 1 GB is already generous

If your run is much shorter than one minute, your processor is faster than ours: create a larger dataset with python make_points.py --n 45000 and use that file for the rest of the exercise.





Task 2: how does it scale?
To find out how the cost grows with the size of the data, we need smaller tests. We create three subsets with the first 25%, 50% and 75% of the points (the first line of the file is the header, hence the + 1):
head -n 7501  points.csv > points_25.csv    # 7,500 points
head -n 15001 points.csv > points_50.csv    # 15,000 points
head -n 22501 points.csv > points_75.csv    # 22,500 points
cp points.csv points_100.csv                # 30,000 points
The points in the file are in random order, so each subset is a representative sample of the whole.
Now run the program on each of them and keep the measurements in a log file. You can use this script, saved as benchmark.sh:
#!/bin/bash
module load languages/python/3.7.12

for size in 25 50 75 100; do
    echo "Testing ${size}% of the data..."
    /usr/bin/time -o timing_results.log -a \
        -f "size=${size}pct wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS_KB=%M" \
        python neighbour_counts.py points_${size}.csv > output_${size}.txt
done

Interactive sessionBatch job


Inside your interactive session:
bash benchmark.sh


Add the Slurm directives (using the account and partition you have for this course) at the top of the script,
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345
#SBATCH --partition=test
#SBATCH --job-name=benchmark
#SBATCH --output=benchmark_out_%j.txt
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --time=00:15:00
and submit it with sbatch benchmark.sh. You can follow it with squeue -u $USER, and when it finishes, look at the statistics with sacct.



The four runs take about four minutes in total. While you wait, think about what you expect: if the time for 25% of the data is T, how long should the 50% run take if the scaling is linear? And if it is quadratic?
When the runs have finished, look at the log:
cat timing_results.log
and fill in this table:










Data used

Time ÷ time at 25%
Peak memory (MB)

Questions




Does the time grow linearly with the number of points? If not, how does it grow? (Compare the ratios with 2×, 3× and 4× for linear scaling, and 4×, 9× and 16× for quadratic scaling.)
How does the peak memory change with the amount of data?
If you had only run the 25% and 50% tests, what time would you have predicted for 100% of the data? How far from the measured time is it?









Solution





Our results (yours will be different in absolute terms, but the ratios should be similar):










Data used
Points
Wall time (s)
Time ÷ time at 25%
Peak memory (MB)




25%

The scaling is quadratic: using 2×, 3× and 4× more points takes about 4×, 9× and 16× longer. This is what we expect from an algorithm that compares every point with every other point (n × n pairs). A straight-line extrapolation would have been badly wrong.
The memory grows only slightly (it is dominated by the Python interpreter, with a small part that grows linearly with the number of points), so it is not a limiting factor for this program.
Assuming linear scaling from the 25% and 50% runs, we would have predicted about 2 × 32.5 s = 65 s for the whole dataset, half of the real time (136 s). With the quadratic model, 8.4 s × 4² = 134 s, within 2% of the measured value.






Task 3: estimate a real project
Suppose now that your project needs to analyse 25 point clouds, each with 60,000 points (twice as many as our dataset), and that you will run them one after the other on a single core each (for example, as an array job with 25 tasks).
Using your measurements and the method of the previous pages:

Estimate the wall-clock time of one run with 60,000 points
Calculate the core-hours of one run and of the whole project
Apply safety factors (use 1.4× for failed jobs, 2.0× for development and 1.2× for the scaling error) and give the total number of core-hours to request
Choose the resources for each job in the array: number of cores, memory and time limit







Solution





Using our measurements (136 s for 30,000 points) and the quadratic scaling, doubling the number of points makes each run 2² = 4 times longer:

Time per run: 136 s × 4 = 544 s, about 9 minutes
Core-hours per run: 544 s × 1 core ÷ 3600 = 0.15 core-hours. For 25 runs: 0.15 × 25 = 3.8 core-hours
Safety factors: 1.4 × 2.0 × 1.2 = 3.36, so 3.8 × 3.36 = about 13 core-hours to request
For each job: 1 core (the program does not use more), memory 1 GB (the program needs about 20 MB, so this is already a very generous margin), and a time limit of, for example, 20 minutes, which is twice the 9 minutes expected. The jobs are short, so they should start quickly

Had we used the straight-line (linear) extrapolation, we would have requested half of the time and the jobs would have run out of time.





Extension A: does it use several cores well?
The program has an option, --workers, to share the work between several processes. Run it with 1, 2 and 4 workers on the 50% dataset (in an allocation with at least 4 cores) and measure the speed-up and the efficiency:
for workers in 1 2 4; do
    /usr/bin/time -o scaling_results.log -a \
        -f "workers=${workers} wall=%e user=%U sys=%S maxRSS_KB=%M" \
        python neighbour_counts.py points_50.csv --workers $workers > /dev/null
done










Workers
Wall time (s)
Speed-up \(T(1)/T(N)\)
Efficiency \(S/N\)
CPU time (s)




1

Questions




How well does the program scale with the number of workers?
Does the total CPU time change when you add workers? What does that mean for the core-hours of a run?
With the quadratic scaling in mind, what would you choose for the 25-run project of Task 3: one core per run, or several cores?









Hints





On a 2-core test machine we measured 32.5 s with one worker and 16.8 s with two workers: a speed-up of 1.9 and an efficiency of 96%, with the CPU time (user) staying the same, about 33 s. When efficiency is this high, the core-hours barely change with the number of cores, so using more cores is a way of getting the results sooner. With 25 independent runs you can also get this by running them at the same time, so one core per run is simple and efficient; use several cores only if you need each result quickly.
How far the efficiency drops with 4 workers depends on the number of physical cores in your node: if some of them are busy with other users’ jobs, or if you asked for fewer cores than workers, the time will not improve.





Extension B: when does memory matter?
By default the program does not keep the list of neighbours of each point, only their number. With the option --store-neighbours it keeps them, and if you also increase the search radius, the number of neighbours grows very quickly. Run the 25% and 50% datasets again with
/usr/bin/time -f "wall=%e maxRSS_KB=%M" \
    python neighbour_counts.py points_25.csv --radius 0.2 --store-neighbours
(and the same with points_50.csv). How does the peak memory grow now? What would you expect for 100% of the data, and what would you request for it in a job script?






Hints





In our test the peak memory grew from 71 MB (25%) to 245 MB (50%): the memory now grows with the number of pairs of neighbouring points, so it also scales quadratically with the number of points. Doubling the data again (100%) multiplies the memory by about 4 once more: we measured 935 MB, nearly 1 GB, where a request of 1 GB would have been too tight and the job would have been killed. With a margin, 2 GB would be the sensible request for this case. Not every program has a flat memory profile: always check how the memory grows as well as the time.





What have we learned?

A small dataset does not mean a cheap calculation: the cost depends on the algorithm, and here it grows with the square of the number of points
Measuring with 3 or 4 sizes shows the scaling that you would not guess from a single test
Wall time, CPU time and peak memory tell you how many cores to use and how much memory to ask for
Converting the results into a request needs the extrapolation to the full problem, the number of runs and some safety factors

Resources

title: What are HPC Systems?
text:
High Performance Computing (HPC) systems are specialized computing environments designed to solve computationally intensive problems that require significant processing power, memory, or storage resources.



Example of different client connecting to an HPC system for remote computing



Key Characteristics of HPC Systems
Parallel Processing: HPC systems typically consist of multiple compute nodes (individual computers) connected via high-speed networks, allowing tasks to be distributed across many processors simultaneously.
Shared Resources: Unlike personal computers, HPC systems are shared among multiple users, requiring job scheduling systems to manage resource allocation fairly and efficiently.
Specialized Hardware: HPC clusters often include:

Multiple CPU cores per node
Large amounts of RAM (64GB-1TB+ per node)
High-speed interconnects
Specialized processors (GPUs for certain workloads)
High-performance storage systems

Batch Processing: Most HPC work is submitted as “jobs” to a queue, rather than running interactively.


When to Use HPC
Consider using HPC systems when your computational tasks involve:

Long-running calculations
Large memory requirements
Parallel processing opportunities
Large datasets that don’t fit on personal computers

title: Benchmarking on HPC systems
text:
Timings from your laptop are a useful first hint, but they can be very different from what you will get on the cluster: different processors, different file systems and different software. The benchmarks that you will use to estimate your request should be run on the system (and the type of node) you will use for the real work.






Never benchmark on the login nodes



Login nodes are shared by everybody and are only meant for editing files, submitting jobs and light tasks. Always run your benchmarks on compute nodes, either through an interactive session or by submitting a batch job. As well as being unfair to other users, timings taken on a busy login node are not reliable.



Interactive benchmarking
An interactive session gives you a shell on a compute node, which is handy for quick tests and for trying out different options:
# Request an interactive session (30 minutes, 4 cores, 8 GB of memory)
salloc --partition=test --nodes=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G --time=00:30:00

# Once the resources are allocated, run your benchmark
srun --cpu-bind=cores /usr/bin/time -v python my_program.py --input test_data.csv
Use sinfo to check which partitions are available in your system (see the job scheduler page).


Batch job benchmarking
For systematic benchmarks (several data sizes, several repetitions, several core counts) it is better to write a job script, so that the tests are reproducible and you keep a record of exactly what you asked for:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345
#SBATCH --partition=test
#SBATCH --job-name=benchmark
#SBATCH --output=benchmark_out_%j.txt
#SBATCH --error=benchmark_err_%j.txt
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00

module load languages/python/3.7.12

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK   # match the requested CPUs

echo "Starting benchmark at $(date)"
echo "Running on node: $(hostname)"

srun --cpu-bind=cores /usr/bin/time -v \
    python my_program.py --input test_10pct.csv --threads $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK






Note



Notice that /usr/bin/time comes after srun, so that it measures your program rather than the srun launcher. The report written by time -v ends up in the job’s error file (benchmark_err_JOBID.txt).




Analysing completed jobs
The scheduler keeps its own record of the resources that each job used, which you can query with sacct:
# Get the job statistics
sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,Elapsed,TotalCPU,MaxRSS,ReqCPUS,State -P
An example of the output (illustrative):
JobID|Elapsed|TotalCPU|MaxRSS|ReqCPUS|State
12345|00:15:30|01:58:45||8|COMPLETED
12345.0|00:15:30|01:58:45|2048000K|8|COMPLETED






Tip



The peak memory (MaxRSS) is reported on the job steps (the lines like 12345.0 or 12345.batch) rather than in the first line of the job. If it is installed in your system, the seff JOBID command gives you a quick summary of the CPU and memory efficiency of a finished job.



Resource analysis
From the output above:








Quantity
Value
How




Wall time
15.5 minutes
Elapsed


CPU time
118.75 minutes
TotalCPU = 1 h 58 min 45 s


Peak memory
about 2 GB
MaxRSS


Core-hours
2.07 core-hours
15.5 min ÷ 60 × 8 cores


CPU efficiency
about 96%
CPU time ÷ (wall time × cores) = 118.75 ÷ (15.5 × 8)



An efficiency close to 100% means that the 8 cores we asked for were busy all the time. If it had been, say, 25%, we would be reserving four times more cores than the program makes use of.



Estimating GPU time requirements
The same benchmarking principles used for CPU-based tasks apply to GPU workloads, but there are some additional things to consider:

GPUs often have longer warm-up times (loading libraries, moving data and the model to the GPU, compiling kernels), so very short tests can be misleading
The batch size, the data transfer overhead between CPU and GPU memory and the GPU memory usage can significantly affect the runtime
Benchmarks should be run with sufficiently large datasets to reflect realistic performance







Check how your system accounts for GPU time



The resource units are not the same in every system. For example, on Isambard-AI, using 1 GPU for 1 hour is counted as 0.25 hours of resource use. Always check the documentation of the facility you are using before converting your estimates into a request.


Converting benchmarks to resource requests

title: Understanding HPC resources
text:
Before asking for time on an HPC system, you need to know how much you will need. Ask for too little and your jobs will be killed half way through; ask for too much and you will wait longer in the queue and waste a shared resource. This second part of the course shows you how to estimate the resources your project needs, starting from small, representative tests.

Intended learning outcomes
By the end of this part, you will:

Understand the key HPC resource concepts: wall-clock time, CPU time and core-hours
Know how to run representative benchmarks of your code
Be able to use simple command-line tools to measure time and memory
Be able to convert benchmark timings into a realistic resource request



Prerequisites

Basic familiarity with the command line and the job scheduler (see the previous part)
A computational task you want to benchmark



Key definitions
HPC allocations are usually measured in core-hours:
\[
\text{core-hours} \approx \text{wall-clock time (hours)} \times \text{number of CPU cores}
\]







Term
Meaning




Wall-clock time
Elapsed time, as measured by a stopwatch


CPU time
Time the processors were actively working for you (excludes waiting for I/O)


Task
One independent run of your code (one simulation, one dataset, …)


Job
What you submit to the scheduler; it may contain many tasks









Example



A program that runs for 2 hours using 8 cores uses 2 × 8 = 16 core-hours.




CPU time versus wall time
The relationship between CPU time and wall-clock time tells you a lot about how your program behaves:

Single core: CPU time ≈ wall time
Multiple cores: CPU time ≈ wall time × number of cores in use
I/O heavy (lots of reading and writing files, waiting for the network): wall time > CPU time

The Linux tool /usr/bin/time -v reports all of these. An example of its output:
Elapsed (wall clock) time (h:mm:ss or m:ss): 0:02:15
User time (seconds): 120.45
System time (seconds): 12.33
Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 2048000
Here the wall-clock time is 2 min 15 s (135 s) and the CPU time is the user plus system time (132.8 s), so the program was busy almost all the time on a single core. The maximum resident set size is the peak memory used: about 2 GB.






Tip



Understanding this relationship helps you optimise your resource requests: if the CPU time is much lower than the wall time multiplied by the cores you asked for, you are reserving cores that are sitting idle.




Why measure rather than guess?



Common mistakes

Ignoring that HPC cores may be faster (or slower!) than your laptop
“My laptop takes 1 hour, so I need 100 hours for 100 runs”: this ignores that the runs can be done at the same time
Missing parallelisation opportunities
Forgetting that there is some overhead in scheduling and starting jobs




Best practice

Benchmark on the target system
Use representative data
Measure actual resource usage
Account for variability between runs






Scaling laws

How does runtime grow with the amount of data?
The way the runtime grows when the problem gets bigger decides how you can extrapolate from a small test to the full problem.



Linear and quadratic growth of the runtime










Pattern
Behaviour
Typical example




Linear, O(n)
2 × data → 2 × time
Processing each file or record independently. Safe to extrapolate


Quadratic, O(n²)
2 × data → 4 × time
All-pairs comparisons, e.g. distance between every pair of points





Testing your scaling
Run your program with increasing fractions of your data and compare the times:
./my_program --data 2percent_sample.csv   # measure time
./my_program --data 4percent_sample.csv   # should take ~2x longer if linear
./my_program --data 8percent_sample.csv   # should take ~4x longer if linear






Warning



If the 8% sample takes 10× longer than the 2% sample (instead of 4×), you do not have linear scaling, and a straight-line extrapolation will underestimate the time needed for the full dataset.





Parallel scaling
When your code can use several cores, the time does not usually shrink in proportion to the number of cores. There are two ways of looking at this:

Strong scaling: keep the problem size fixed and add cores. How much faster does it get?
Weak scaling: increase the problem size in proportion to the number of cores. Does the runtime stay the same?

For strong scaling we define the speed-up and the parallel efficiency on \(N\) cores as
\[
S(N) = \frac{T(1)}{T(N)}, \qquad E(N) = \frac{S(N)}{N} = \frac{T(1)}{N \, T(N)}
\]
where \(T(N)\) is the wall-clock time using \(N\) cores.

Amdahl’s law
Every program has some part that cannot run in parallel (reading the input, setting things up, …). If a fraction \(p\) of the work can be parallelised, the best possible speed-up on \(N\) cores is
\[
S(N) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + p/N}
\]
So even if 90% of your code is parallel (\(p = 0.9\)), you can never go more than 10× faster, however many cores you use.


Testing parallel scaling
#!/bin/bash
dataset="my_data.csv"

for cores in 1 2 4 8 16; do
    echo "Testing with $cores cores..."
    /usr/bin/time -f "cores=$cores wall=%E cpu=%U+%S" \
        my_parallel_program --input $dataset --threads $cores \
        2>> scaling_results.log
done

Efficiency

title: Job scheduler
text:
Introduction to Slurm
Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is a job scheduling system used by many HPC clusters to manage computational resources fairly among users.

Key Slurm Concepts
Jobs: Computational tasks submitted to the scheduler
Nodes: Individual computers in the cluster
Partitions/Queues: Groups of nodes with similar characteristics
Allocation: Resources (nodes, CPUs, memory) assigned to your job



Submitting Jobs
# Submit a job script
sbatch myjob.slurm

Basic Job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345
#SBATCH --partition=test
#SBATCH --job-name=my_serial_job
#SBATCH --output=output_%j.txt
#SBATCH --error=error_%j.txt
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=4G


# Load required modules
module load languages/python/3.7.12

# Change to working directory
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# Run your program
python my_analysis.py






Loading modules



You need to load the software you need. You can list the modules available with
module avail
and load them with load option, e.g.
module load languages/python/3.7.12




Important Slurm Directives








Directive
Purpose
Example




--account
Project name to use
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345


--partition
Queue/partition to use
#SBATCH --partition=compute


--job-name
Set job name
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis


--time
Maximum runtime
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00


--nodes
Number of nodes
#SBATCH --nodes=2


--ntasks
Number of tasks/processes
#SBATCH --ntasks=8


--cpus-per-task
CPUs per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4


--mem
Memory per node
#SBATCH --mem=32G


--mem-per-cpu
Memory per CPU
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G


--gres
Generic resources (GPUs)
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2






Managing Jobs

Checking System Status
# View available partitions/queues
sinfo

# View node information  
sinfo -N -l

# Check your job queue
squeue -u $USER

# Check all jobs in system
squeue

# View detailed job information
scontrol show job JOBID


Monitoring Jobs
# Check status of specific job
squeue -j JOBID

# Check your running jobs
squeue -u $USER -t RUNNING

# Check your pending jobs  
squeue -u $USER -t PENDING

# Get detailed job information
scontrol show job JOBID

# View job accounting information
sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,MaxRSS,Elapsed


Controlling Jobs
# Cancel a job
scancel JOBID

# Cancel all your jobs
scancel -u $USER

# Cancel jobs by name
scancel --name=my_job_name

# Hold a pending job
scontrol hold JOBID

# Release a held job
scontrol release JOBID



Array Jobs
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345
#SBATCH --partition=test
#SBATCH --job-name=array_job
#SBATCH --output=array_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --error=array_%A_%a.err
#SBATCH --array=1-100
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G

# Use array task ID to process different input files
input_file="input_${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.txt"
output_file="output_${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.txt"

# Load required modules
module load languages/python/3.7.12

# Run analysis on this array element
python process_data.py $input_file $output_file


GPU Jobs
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=ABC012345
#SBATCH --partition=gpu_short
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_job
#SBATCH --output=gpu_output_%j.txt
#SBATCH --error=gpu_error_%j.txt
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=16G

# Load required modules
module load languages/python/3.7.12

# Load CUDA module
module load cuda/11.8.0-rgxs

# Run GPU program
python my_gpu_script.py

title: Best practices
text:
Best Practices

Resource Estimation

Start small: Test with shorter time limits and smaller resource requests
Monitor usage: Use sacct and seff to check actual resource utilization
Right-size requests: Don’t over-request resources you won’t use



Job Organization

Use descriptive job names and organize output files
Include error checking in your scripts
Use arrays for parameter sweeps rather than submitting many individual jobs
Clean up: Remove unnecessary output files periodically



Example Resource Check
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=resource_check
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=1G

# Print system information
echo "Job started at: $(date)"
echo "Running on node: $(hostname)"
echo "Number of CPUs: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"
echo "Memory allocated: $SLURM_MEM_PER_NODE MB"

# Your actual work here
python my_script.py

echo "Job finished at: $(date)"



Getting Help

System Documentation

Check your HPC system’s documentation website
Look for system-specific examples and policies
Review partition/queue descriptions and limits



Useful Commands for Troubleshooting
# Check system limits
scontrol show config

# View partition details
scontrol show partition PARTITION_NAME

# Check node specifications
scontrol show nodes

# View your account associations
sacctmgr show associations user=$USER



Common Issues
Job doesn’t start: Check resource requests against partition limits
Job fails immediately: Verify paths, modules, and permissions
Out of memory errors: Increase memory request or optimize code
Time limit exceeded: Increase time request or optimize algorithms
Remember: HPC systems vary between institutions, so always consult your local documentation and support staff for system-specific guidance.

title: Shell scripts
text:
So far, we have been running things directly on the command line, “interactively”. However, you might want to keep your commands in a file, and be able to run, share, modify, or use files as templates. This is the gateway to coding and is great practice for developing your reproducible work.
A script is a file of instructions that can be directly read and run by a program. In our case, we are going to make a script in shell language.
Let’s create a very simple script. Open nano creating a file called first_script.sh and include the lines
#!/bin/bash

ls -l *soft
echo "That is all of the files with \"soft\" in that I could find here."
It is a good practice to always start your scripts with a shebang line like #!/bin/bash, that tells the system to run the correct shell for the script.
Shell scripts need to have execution permission, so it is important to remember to make your scripts executable with chmod +x script.sh. Once done it, we can run our first script with
./first_script.sh

Variables and structures
Scripts can also have variables, conditional structures and loops. While a deep dive into these concepts is beyond the scope of an introductory course, it is worth mentioning them to understand all the basic capabilities of shell scripting.
Use descriptive variable names:
user_name="John"
echo "Hello, ${user_name}!"
Make decisions using if-then-else statements:
if [[ "$1" == "help" ]]; then
  echo "Usage: script.sh [option]"
elif [[ "$1" == "version" ]]; then
  echo "Version 1.0"
else
  echo "Unknown option"
fi
Allow repetition of commands for a specified number of iterations or over a list of items:
for file in *.txt; do
  echo "Processing ${file}"
done
